questions.question: The Euler tour algorithm is applied to a connected undirected network in which every vertex has even degree. Which description matches its steps?
options: Visit every vertex once in a closed route, then add each remaining edge as a back-and-forth trip.
Traverse edges one at a time in any order, and only at the end check that the route has closed up.
Find closed excursions of unused edges, then join them by adding new edges between their start vertices.
Close an unused-edge walk at the start, then splice in closed unused-edge excursions until done.

questions.question: In the Euler tour algorithm on a connected undirected network in which every vertex has even degree, the first walk starts at $s$ and follows unused edges. Why can it never get stuck at a vertex $v\ne s$?
options: The network is connected, so from every vertex some path leads back to $s$ along unused edges.
Every vertex has degree exactly 2, so the walk enters and leaves each vertex exactly once.
Each arrival at $v$ leaves an odd number of unused edges there, so one is left to leave by.
The walk never returns to a vertex it has already visited, so fresh edges are always available.

questions.question: The Euler tour algorithm is to be applied to a connected undirected network in which every vertex has even degree with at least one edge. Which vertices may serve as the start vertex $s$?
options: Any vertex, but every choice leads to the same Euler tour.
Only a vertex of degree 2, so the first cycle closes.
Any vertex, since each has an edge and even degree.
Only a vertex of odd degree, as the tour leaves it.

questions.question: In the Euler tour algorithm, $\Omega$ is the current closed tour and $\Omega_1$ is a closed traversal of unused edges that starts and ends at a vertex $v$ on $\Omega$. What does splicing $\Omega_1$ into $\Omega$ at $v$ produce?
options: Follow $\Omega$ to $v$, go round $\Omega_1$ back to $v$, then finish $\Omega$.
Follow all of $\Omega$ back to its start, then go round $\Omega_1$ from there.
Replace the part of $\Omega$ around $v$ by $\Omega_1$ to keep the tour short.
Join the start of $\Omega$ to $v$ by an added edge, then go round $\Omega_1$.

questions.question: The Euler tour algorithm is applied to a network in which some pairs of vertices are joined by two parallel edges. Why must the used edges be recorded by their identity rather than by the pair of vertices they join?
options: Parallel copies have different lengths, so they must be told apart.
Each parallel copy is its own edge, to be used exactly once.
Once one copy is used, its twin may be skipped as a duplicate.
Each parallel copy may be traversed in one direction only.

questions.question: During the first walk of the Euler tour algorithm, a vertex $v\ne s$ of degree 6 has so far been entered twice and left once; the walk is now at $v$. How many unused edges does $v$ have now?
options: 4 unused edges, since only arrivals use edges
5 unused edges, since only departures use edges
3 unused edges, so the walk can leave $v$
2 unused edges, since each visit used two edges

questions.question: A network has edges $P$–$Q$, $Q$–$R$, $R$–$S$, $S$–$P$, $Q$–$T$, $T$–$U$, $U$–$Q$, $R$–$X$, $X$–$Y$, $Y$–$R$. The Euler tour algorithm has built $\Omega=$ $P$–$Q$–$R$–$S$–$P$. At which vertices can the next closed excursion $\Omega_1$ start?
options: At $T$ or at $X$
At $Q$ or at $R$
At $P$ or at $S$
At any vertex of $\Omega$

questions.question: In the complete network on vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ (one edge between every pair), the first walk of the Euler tour algorithm starts at $A$, always takes the unused edge to the alphabetically first neighbour, and stops on returning to $A$. Which closed traversal $\Omega$ results?

A network has two parallel edges $e_1$, $e_2$ between $A$ and $B$ and the triangle $B$–$C$–$D$–$B$. The Euler tour algorithm starts at $A$, uses $e_1$ to $B$ and returns to $A$ by $e_2$. Is this first closed traversal valid, and can the algorithm be completed?
options: No; it uses the edge $A$–$B$ twice.
No; a cycle needs at least three vertices.
Yes; but the triangle can no longer be added.
Yes; later the triangle is spliced in at $B$.

questions.question: The Euler tour algorithm has built $\Omega=$ $P$–$Q$–$R$–$P$ and then the closed excursion $\Omega_1=$ $P$–$S$–$T$–$P$ of unused edges. Which tour results from splicing $\Omega_1$ into $\Omega$ at $P$?
Two students run the Euler tour algorithm on the same connected network with all degrees even, but make different eligible choices and obtain different closed sequences of vertices. What follows?
options: Both sequences are Euler tours of the network.
At most one is correct; the other reused an edge.
Only the run with the fewest splices is valid.
Both are valid, but the longer one has more splices.

questions.question: In the Euler tour algorithm on a connected undirected network in which every vertex has even degree, the first closed traversal $\Omega$ has been built. What holds for the edges not used by $\Omega$?
options: At every vertex, an odd number of them remain.
At every vertex, an even number of them remain.
Only vertices off $\Omega$ keep an even count.
Every vertex on $\Omega$ has none of them left.

questions.question: In the Euler tour algorithm, $\Omega$ is the current closed tour. Why must the next closed excursion $\Omega_1$ of unused edges start at a vertex that lies on $\Omega$?
options: The two routes must share a vertex, where $\Omega_1$ is inserted into $\Omega$.
Vertices off $\Omega$ have odd degree, so no closed excursion can start there.
Only vertices on $\Omega$ have unused edges, so there is nowhere else to start.
$\Omega_1$ must avoid every vertex of $\Omega$ except one, to keep edges distinct.

questions.question: A network consists of the triangles $A$–$B$–$C$ and $C$–$D$–$E$, sharing $C$. The Euler tour algorithm has built $\Omega=$ $A$–$B$–$C$–$A$ and the excursion $\Omega_1=$ $C$–$D$–$E$–$C$. Which tour results from splicing $\Omega_1$ into $\Omega$ at $C$?

A network has edges $P$–$Q$, $Q$–$R$, $R$–$S$, $S$–$P$, $Q$–$S$, $Q$–$T$, $S$–$T$. The Euler tour algorithm has built $\Omega=$ $P$–$Q$–$R$–$S$–$P$. Which closed traversal can it splice in next, starting at $Q$?
A network consists of the cycles $A$–$B$–$C$–$D$–$A$ and $A$–$E$–$C$–$F$–$A$ (8 edges). Which sequence is a valid final output of the Euler tour algorithm for this network?
The Euler tour algorithm always succeeds on a connected undirected network in which every vertex has even degree. What does this success establish about such networks?
options: Even degrees are necessary for any network to have an Euler tour.
The Euler tour of such a network is unique once a start is fixed.
An Euler tour exists whenever at most two vertex degrees are odd.
Even degrees plus connectedness are sufficient for an Euler tour.

questions.question: Run on a connected undirected network in which every vertex has even degree, the Euler tour algorithm repeatedly splices closed excursions into the current tour. Why does it end with a tour that uses every edge?
options: Each round adds one new vertex, so after as many rounds as vertices all edges are used.
Each round lowers every degree by 2, until every vertex has degree 0 left.
Each round uses new edges; while some remain, connectedness puts one at a tour vertex.
Each round closes at its start, so after one round from each vertex nothing is left.

questions.question: A network consists of the triangle $A$–$B$–$C$ and the separate triangle $D$–$E$–$F$, with no edge between them; every degree is 2. The Euler tour algorithm starts at $A$ and builds $\Omega=$ $A$–$B$–$C$–$A$. What happens next?
options: $\Omega_1=$ $D$–$E$–$F$–$D$ is appended, giving the tour $A$–$B$–$C$–$A$–$D$–$E$–$F$–$D$.
The algorithm restarts from $D$ and merges both cycles into one tour.
The algorithm is finished, since $\Omega$ is closed and degrees are even.
No vertex of $\Omega$ has an unused edge, so no Euler tour can be completed.

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$, $B$–$C$, $C$–$D$, $D$–$B$, so $A$ has degree 1 and $B$ degree 3. Ignoring the even-degree requirement, the first walk of the Euler tour algorithm starts at $A$ and follows unused edges. Where does the walk stop, whatever choices are made?
options: Back at $A$, after the triangle
Stuck at $B$, never back at $A$
Stuck at $C$ or at $D$, by choice
Stuck at $B$, on first arrival
